title: Crisman Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Crisman wells have a 285-foot median depth, with fractured-bedrock drilling commonly costing $65-$100 per foot.
h1: Crisman, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Crisman is a mountain well area where most permitted wells draw from unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers. Records within five miles show a 285-foot median well depth, a median reported yield of 7.0 gallons per minute, and a median static water level 60 feet below the surface.

Those figures are useful for planning, but they do not guarantee what a particular lot will produce. Mountain bedrock can change quickly across short distances. Before buying or building near Mountain Meadows, Sunshine, Tall Timber, Seven Hills, Sugarloaf, or Gold Hill, review nearby permits, well construction records, water levels, and the legal water use allowed for the property.

sections.heading: Crisman well depths reflect fractured mountain bedrock
sections.html:
Among the permitted wells near Crisman that report total depth, the median is 285 feet. The middle half runs from 155 to 425 feet, so a driller bidding a new well here should not assume every hole will resemble a shallow foothills well. The 90th-percentile depth is 600 feet, and the deepest record reaches 1,402 feet.

Depth records are spread across the area: 16% are under 100 feet, 35% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 37% between 300 and 600 feet, and 12% are 600 feet or deeper. Most permits name unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. Granite and gneiss fractures control where water is found, so the final depth can differ substantially between neighboring lots.

sections.heading: What a Crisman well may produce
sections.html:
The reported median yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 5.0 and 10.0 gallons per minute. That is generally a workable range for a household well, but the pumping test and storage system still matter. A well's reported yield is not the same as unlimited daily water use.

Only 3% of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute. Another 18% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while 70% are between 5 and 15 gallons per minute and 10% exceed 15 gallons per minute. A buyer should ask how long the test ran, whether the result was measured after drilling, and how the home will manage storage during peak demand.

sections.heading: Crisman water levels and the long record
sections.html:
Static water level means the depth from the ground surface down to standing water in the well. The local median is 60 feet, with the middle half between 18 and 100 feet. That range affects pump setting, electrical planning, and the amount of lift a system must handle.

The decade figures vary rather than forming a simple, steady decline: 30 feet in the 1960s, 40 feet in the 1970s, 68 feet in the 1980s, 6 feet in the 2000s, 90 feet in the 2010s, and 100 feet in the 2020s. Because only 125 wells report static water levels, the series is a warning to check the individual well and nearby records, not proof of one uniform water-table trend.

sections.heading: Crisman drilling history and local contractors
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records show permits from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025. Permit activity was highest in the 1970s, with 861 permits, followed by 552 in the 1980s, 557 in the 1990s, 300 in the 2000s, 186 in the 2010s, and 114 in the 2020s. The records include 3,765 permitted wells, with 2,480 recorded as constructed.

The most frequent driller name is Ground Water Systems Inc. (Wilson, Richard R.), appearing on 862 records. Ingram Drilling Inc. (Ingram, Stephen E.) appears on 268, and Norris & Sons (Norris, T A) on 201. These records show local history, not an endorsement. Confirm current licensing, insurance, availability, and what each bid includes.

sections.heading: Expected cost to drill a Crisman well
sections.html:
Fractured granite and gneiss make drilling cost sensitive to depth and ground conditions. The local cost model uses $65-$100 per foot. At the 285-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $18,500-$28,500.

A finished system, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is modeled at about $24,500-$40,500 at that median depth. Treat this as a planning range, not a guaranteed quote. Ask the driller to separate drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, testing, trenching, electrical work, and any difficult access or extra-depth charges. A low initial bid can change if the hole must continue through unproductive bedrock.

sections.heading: Crisman risks to check before construction
sections.html:
Low yield and dry holes are the main physical risks in fractured mountain rock. The records show that most reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, but some produce under 1 gallon per minute. A buyer should obtain the well permit, construction report, yield test, water-quality results, and maintenance history rather than relying on a neighbor's experience.

Environmental review also matters. Within about 10 miles, the mapped record includes 78 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 746 historic mine features, and 65 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not automatically mean a particular well is contaminated. Test the actual water and check the site's proximity to mines, cleanup areas, septic systems, and drainage. Confirm casing, grout, wellhead protection, septic setbacks, access, and the building site's legal water use before committing.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Crisman, Colorado?
faq.a: The median permitted well depth within five miles of Crisman is 285 feet. The middle half runs from 155 to 425 feet, while 12% of wells are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest record is 1,402 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make depth unpredictable, so nearby well records are useful when planning a bid.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Crisman?
faq.a: The local drilling model is $65-$100 per foot. At the 285-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $18,500-$28,500. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $24,500-$40,500. A contractor should confirm access, casing, grout, testing, and possible extra-depth charges.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Crisman?
faq.a: Reported well yield has a 7.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half between 5.0 and 10.0 gallons per minute. Three percent of reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute. Ask for the actual pumping test and plan storage carefully, because a tested yield is not the same as unrestricted household consumption.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Crisman?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that every Crisman well is safe to drink. Nearby mapped environmental records include 78 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 746 historic mine features, and 65 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the individual well for relevant contaminants, review its history, and maintain treatment based on the results.

faq.q: Are Crisman wells getting deeper or running lower?
faq.a: Reported static water levels vary by measurement decade: 30 feet in the 1960s, 40 feet in the 1970s, 68 feet in the 1980s, 6 feet in the 2000s, 90 feet in the 2010s, and 100 feet in the 2020s. Only 125 wells report levels, so this is not proof of a uniform decline. Check nearby, comparable wells.
